segments.title: Why the French fleet changes the Allied balance
segments.body: This counterfactual begins with the French Navy remaining on the Allied side after France falls. The fleet is more than a list of hulls because it connects France to overseas bases and helps sustain the French Empire. In the 1939 deployment survey, Dunkerque, Strasbourg, Béarn, Georges Leygues, Montcalm, and Gloire anchor an Atlantic force at Brest. Toulon contributes Algérie, Dupleix, Colbert, De Grasse, Tourville, and other cruisers for the Mediterranean. Capital ships, cruisers, torpilleurs d’escadre, and contre-torpilleurs form balanced task groups rather than isolated reinforcements. In scale and capability, the fleet is broadly comparable to Italy's Regia Marina, so its continued Allied service largely offsets Italian naval strength and changes Royal Navy calculations. France's fall remains a major strategic loss. At sea, however, it is less decisive, while Anglo-French planning had failed to prepare either ally for the other's collapse.

evidence.note: The transcript frames the scenario, the French Empire, and the fleet's Brest and Toulon force structure.
The French and Italian navies are compared as broadly equivalent in size, strength, and capability.

segments.summary: A fully Allied French Navy restores the force balance assumed in Anglo-French war plans and offsets much of Italy's naval weight.

segments.title: Béarn as an Atlantic escort carrier
segments.body: Béarn combined a compromised carrier design with politically driven machinery changes, leaving her ill suited to front-line fleet operations. Individually plausible aircraft-handling ideas accumulated without forming a coherent whole. In this scenario she could still serve as an escort carrier. Aircraft aboard her could support convoys and anti-submarine patrols in the North Atlantic or Arctic. Trade protection demands less speed and striking power than a Mediterranean fleet operation, giving the ship a useful second-line role.

evidence.note: Bearn is discussed as a possible escort carrier supporting Atlantic convoys and ASW aircraft.

segments.summary: Béarn's flaws rule out front-line fleet-carrier work. She could still carry anti-submarine aircraft for Atlantic and Arctic convoy escort.

segments.title: Using older French battleships for second-line duties
segments.body: Courbet- and Bretagne-class battleships were obsolete beside modern capital ships. Their useful jobs lay in shore bombardment, amphibious support, convoy protection, and guarding confined waters. Geography can make a slow battleship dangerous when an attacker cannot use speed to avoid it. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau illustrate the problem: meeting even an old battleship with a convoy would force them either to abandon the attack or risk damage far from repair. Any damage would make a raider easier for faster Allied pursuers to catch, so second-line ships could still restrict German options.

evidence.note: The Courbet and Bretagne classes in convoy, bombardment, and chokepoint roles.

segments.summary: Even obsolescent Courbet and Bretagne-class battleships could protect convoys, support landings, and complicate enemy operations in narrow waters.

segments.title: Bases, submarines, and the French supply problem
segments.body: French forces at Bizerte, Oran, the Levant, Casablanca, Indochina, and other stations give the scenario a worldwide footprint. The large French submarine force was well suited to Mediterranean operations. Historically, Britain had to draw submarines from the Far East and Indian Ocean while building up its own force, exposing boats designed for those distant stations to narrow, shallow waters for which they were ill suited. Continued French participation could reduce that pressure. Losing metropolitan France would still cause a severe logistical shock because French weapons, ammunition, and spare parts were incompatible with British systems. Overseas facilities and stockpiles could sustain operations temporarily, while longer service would require new Allied supply chains for specialised French matériel.

evidence.note: French overseas bases and a large submarine force could reduce pressure on British deployments, although incompatible French weapons, ammunition, and spare parts would require new Allied supply chains.

segments.summary: French overseas bases and submarines could ease British deployments, although the loss of metropolitan supply facilities would leave specialised ammunition and spares to replace.

segments.title: Surcouf and the cost of an intermediate design
segments.body: Surcouf's cruiser-submarine concept is criticised as an attractive paper solution whose practical value fails to justify the compromise. The comparison is a 10-inch gun, judged to offer roughly the rate of fire of a 12-inch or even a 14-inch weapon without enough cost saving to justify choosing it. If cost is the priority, a 9.2-inch weapon is presented as a faster-firing alternative with better value. The criticism concerns whether an intermediate design earns its place through useful performance. It leaves the rest of France's large submarine force as capable offensive and defensive assets, particularly in the Mediterranean.

evidence.note: The cruiser-submarine concept is compared with 10-inch guns, larger weapons with similar rates of fire, and a faster-firing 9.2-inch alternative.
The discussion returns to cruiser submarines, then distinguishes France's useful conventional submarine force.

segments.summary: A comparison with 10-inch guns explains the criticism of Surcouf: an intermediate design must justify its cost through useful performance.

segments.title: The scale of the French fleet in 1939
segments.body: The prewar inventory includes two fast Dunkerque-class battleships and seven Courbet- and Bretagne-class battleships. It also counts seven heavy cruisers, eleven light cruisers, 32 contre-torpilleurs, 38 torpilleurs d'escadre, and 83 submarines. The cruiser survey names the Duquesne and Suffren classes, Algérie, Jeanne d'Arc, Émile Bertin, and the minelayer Pluton. The force mixes modern striking units with escorts, patrol vessels, and second-line capital ships. A seaplane tender also offers the ability to move into position and establish a fixed base. France could not dominate at sea alone, but this fleet was large enough to alter either coalition's plans.

evidence.note: The transcript inventories the Dunkerque, Courbet, and Bretagne battleships, cruiser forces, destroyer types, and 83 submarines.
An unnamed seaplane tender is described as a mobile asset able to establish a fixed base.
The preceding fleet and deployment survey is explicitly dated to 1939.

segments.summary: The 1939 survey counts two fast battleships, seven older battleships, eighteen cruisers, seventy destroyers, and eighty-three submarines.

segments.title: Why Britain would not gamble on ambiguous French orders
segments.body: The French government treated the navy as a bargaining asset when seeking terms from Nazi Germany, because removing it from the Allied order of battle would seriously weaken Britain. The government's political resolve appears to have failed before the French Army exhausted every capacity to resist, leaving naval commanders with confused and changing instructions. Germany might hesitate to punish a rapid naval defection too severely because renewed French Army resistance could disrupt the victory it wanted to consolidate. Britain could respect the honour of French officers and sailors while remaining unable to predict whether they would obey a later order against their former ally. Dunkerque and Strasbourg might even have been in Plymouth if recently cancelled deployment orders had remained in force, placing two major ships under immediate British control after the armistice. This command-and-trust crisis explains why the counterfactual requires an early fleet-wide decision rather than scattered ships choosing independently.

evidence.note: The French government used the fleet as armistice leverage while issuing wavering orders that left Britain unsure whether French crews would obey a later command against it. Dunkerque and Strasbourg might have been in Plymouth if their recently cancelled deployment orders had remained in force.

segments.summary: The fleet became armistice leverage, and contradictory French orders left Britain unwilling to gamble on its former ally despite respecting French servicemen.

segments.title: What Béarn shows about French naval innovation
segments.body: Béarn separates innovation from an integrated design. Machinery changes, aircraft-handling schemes, political intervention, and other plausible ideas accumulated until they conflicted. The result shows how experimentation can fail when a ship lacks the structure needed to make its parts work together. French naval innovation still produced capable and unusual warships elsewhere, so Béarn does not define the navy's wider design record.

evidence.note: Béarn's accumulated innovations conflicted with one another, while wider French naval experimentation produced other capable designs.

segments.summary: Béarn shows how promising ideas can undermine one another when a design lacks an integrating structure. French experimentation still produced capable warships elsewhere.

segments.title: A Darlan-led fleet evacuation to Britain
segments.body: An all-Free-French outcome requires a senior naval leader with authority across the fleet, and François Darlan is the candidate proposed with that reach. The scenario has him decide around 14 June 1940 and order the ships to leave for British ports by 21 June. He could also load merchant ships with supplies and encourage naval personnel to bring their families. Evacuating families on that scale is judged unlikely, although possible. If the fleet arrived as one force, Britain would receive a coherent Allied partner instead of facing uncertain loyalties among scattered ships. Darlan's seniority and control of the navy would make him the likely leader in exile. Charles de Gaulle would command the ground forces and help secure colonial allegiance, with less political influence than he held historically.

evidence.note: In the proposed scenario, François Darlan orders the French fleet to leave for British ports between 14 and 21 June 1940, then leads the Free French while Charles de Gaulle commands its ground forces.

segments.summary: In this scenario, Darlan orders the fleet to leave for British ports between 14 and 21 June 1940 and becomes the senior Free French leader, with de Gaulle commanding ground forces.

segments.title: Holding the empire and rebuilding supply chains
segments.body: Control of the fleet would strengthen Free French authority across the empire. Colonial officials would have to choose between a Vichy representative with little force and a Free French leadership able to arrive with ships, supplies, and soldiers. Some colonial personnel regarded Vichy as a puppet government, so the departure of the whole fleet would also strengthen Free French claims to national independence. Darlan could send de Gaulle with land and naval forces to bring reluctant territories into the new alignment. Evacuated supplies would buy time to arrange replacement ammunition, shells, and spare parts. France had already been negotiating with American suppliers before defeat, allowing the government in exile to inherit those contracts and expand them for the fleet's greater needs.

evidence.note: Free French control of the fleet could draw colonial authorities toward the government in exile, while existing American contracts offered a basis for replacing ammunition, shells, and spare parts.

segments.summary: A fleet that joins the Allies could help pull French colonial authorities with it, while existing American contracts offer a starting point for replacing specialised supplies.

segments.title: Operation Compass with French pressure from the west
segments.body: The historical Operation Compass began on 9 December 1940, took roughly 130,000 prisoners, and cost Italy most of its deployed tanks, aircraft, and artillery. Wavell held the regional command, while Lieutenant-General Richard O'Connor's Western Desert Force exploited Italian weaknesses in equipment, logistics, and official support. In this scenario the offensive might start earlier because the Allies would not need to resolve the status of French forces at Alexandria. If French North and West African territories join the Free French side, Italian troops must guard their western frontier or attack toward Tunisia and Algeria before moving east. Dividing the force leaves it still more exposed to the Western Desert Force and to French pressure from the rear. French naval interdiction would also make reinforcement and retreat harder. An earlier collapse in Libya could finish the North African campaign before the historical diversion to Greece and leave more Allied forces available for the Greek campaign.

evidence.note: The transcript considers Operation Compass, Italy's western frontier, and coordinated French-British pressure in Libya.

segments.summary: The scenario projects a faster Allied victory in Libya because Italian forces must cover Tunisia and Algeria while French and British forces converge.

segments.title: Malta convoys and the Mediterranean supply corridor
segments.body: Control of North Africa would transform the route used to resupply Malta in this scenario. Convoys could travel along a friendly coast and approach Malta from the south before entering waters nearer Italy. Land-based aircraft could provide fighter cover, strike support, and anti-submarine patrols along the route. This might also reopen the Mediterranean for urgent convoys bound for the Far East. Difficult narrows would remain, but access to air bases along the North African coast would make those passages easier to support.

evidence.note: North African air bases support Malta convoys and could make the Mediterranean usable for urgent Far East traffic, despite difficult narrows.

segments.summary: Allied control of the North African coast could give Malta convoys sustained air support and reopen a Mediterranean supply route toward the Far East.

segments.title: Holding Crete and bringing Axis oil fields within range
segments.body: Greece would probably still fall for the same reasons as in the historical campaign. Crete's fate is judged differently because an Italian fleet under greater pressure would have less freedom to help capture the island. Retaining Crete could put oil fields critical to Germany and Italy within range of heavy bombers. That further effect depends on both keeping the island and being able to operate those bombers there.

evidence.note: The counterfactual distinguishes Greece's probable fall from Crete's possible retention and explicitly conditions attacks on oil fields on operating heavy bombers from the island.

segments.summary: Retaining Crete could give heavy bombers access to Axis oil fields, provided the Allies could operate them from the island.

segments.title: No Mers-el-Kébir and a larger Taranto strike
segments.body: The scenario removes the political crisis that led to Mers-el-Kébir, so Force H would not need to exist in its historical form. French support could leave a third British carrier available for Taranto. That extra capacity would allow Eagle to leave operations for repairs after earlier damage, potentially making all three carriers ready for the raid. Taranto was conceived and developed as a multi-carrier operation, and the additional carrier would restore that intended scale. The projected strike contains 84 Swordfish and 24 Skuas, compared with the 21 of 24 Swordfish that made the historical attack. A larger attack could damage more of the Italian battle fleet, although the outcome remains conditional on aircraft availability and the strike's success.

evidence.note: The scenario avoids Mers-el-Kebir and projects a third carrier, time to repair Eagle, and 84 Swordfish plus 24 Skuas compared with 21 of 24 Swordfish historically.
Taranto is described as conceived, developed, and planned as a multi-carrier operation.

segments.summary: A cooperative French fleet removes the premise for Mers-el-Kébir and may allow a three-carrier Taranto operation against the Italian battle fleet.

segments.title: Extra hulls create maintenance time as well as firepower
segments.body: Operational availability matters more than paper strength. Extra French hulls would let the Royal Navy rotate more of its own vessels through maintenance instead of repeatedly postponing long dockyard periods. Ark Royal is the example: she carried workable but accumulating defects that several weeks in a major yard could have addressed. Deferred maintenance was a major contributor to her vulnerability, although it was not the sole cause of her historical loss. Fleet size therefore generates combat power through repair and rotation as well as through additional guns and aircraft. Sea routes carry logistics and forces between theatres, making maintenance capacity part of sustained naval power.

evidence.note: Additional French hulls would give Britain operational slack to rotate ships through deferred maintenance; Ark Royal exemplifies a vessel that wartime pressure denied a sustained yard period.

segments.summary: An intact French fleet gives Britain operational slack, allowing ships such as Ark Royal to receive overdue dockyard work instead of remaining in continuous service.

segments.title: Giulio Cesare and the limits of a larger Taranto raid
segments.body: If two-thirds of the projected 84 Swordfish carried torpedoes, the enlarged Taranto raid could launch 56 torpedoes. Giulio Cesare is expected to survive because there is virtually no way to line up a torpedo attack against her. A concentrated attack by all 24 Skuas is raised as an alternative, although those aircraft are expected to attack other targets and probably suppress anti-aircraft guns. Heavy damage to the rest of the battle fleet could leave ships beyond repair or out of action for months or years. Italy's limited repair facilities would then restrict how quickly surviving ships could return.

evidence.note: The projected torpedo load, Giulio Cesare's inaccessible torpedo approach, and possible Skua suppression of anti-aircraft guns are discussed.
The larger raid is expected to impose months or years of repair work on Italy's limited facilities.

segments.summary: Torpedo approaches could spare Giulio Cesare even in a much larger Taranto raid, while Italy's repair capacity would limit recovery from damage elsewhere.

segments.title: Atlantic escorts and the U-boat force's early losses
segments.body: Béarn, heavy cruisers, smaller escorts, and French submarines could cover Atlantic convoy routes or free British ships for other tasks. Britain could also reduce surveillance of French ports, although it would probably still keep an eye on them. French submarine strength would let the Royal Navy retain more T-class boats in the Far East instead of withdrawing them to the Mediterranean. Extra sloops and avisos would enter the escort force during the years when Germany's submarine arm was still expanding. Their equipment did not have to surpass British systems to matter because more escorts would deny easy approaches and increase the chance of an early U-boat loss. Losing even a few boats in 1939 or 1940 would remove experienced crews and future instructors from the force's training pipeline. The comparison with German destroyer losses at Narvik shows why early personnel losses can hinder later expansion.

evidence.note: French Atlantic assets, convoy escorts, and the long-term effect of early U-boat losses.

segments.summary: French cruisers, sloops, avisos, and submarines would strengthen Atlantic escort work, where early U-boat losses could have disproportionate long-term effects.

segments.title: Madagascar and the strategic value of colonial alignment
segments.body: In this scenario Madagascar is already Free French, removing the need for a later Allied operation to secure the island against possible Japanese use. Any remaining Vichy-aligned colonies could receive a visit from de Gaulle, land forces, and a naval detachment. In North Africa, Bizerte and Sousse become submarine staging points alongside Malta. Those bases tighten interdiction of Italian reinforcement routes and connect colonial allegiance directly to Mediterranean sea control.

evidence.note: The transcript removes the historical Madagascar operation from the scenario, describes pressure on remaining Vichy colonies, and identifies Bizerte and Sousse as submarine bases.

segments.summary: If French colonies align early with the fleet, the Allies avoid later operations against them and gain bases for Mediterranean interdiction.

segments.title: Could early defeats unseat Mussolini?
segments.body: Naval and colonial reverses could become a political crisis inside Fascist Italy. Mussolini projected more security than he possessed, and open criticism from senior political figures illustrates limits on his authority. A more destructive Taranto strike, the quick collapse of Libya, and failure in Greece could threaten his position or encourage an attempt to seize French territory. A further Italian land grab could provoke French soldiers or civilians against their own government, threatening the settlement Hitler wanted to preserve. Concessions small enough to avoid renewed French resistance might therefore fail to restore Mussolini's standing. German intervention could still defeat Greece because it attacked where Greek defences were weaker. Allied control of North Africa and a diminished Regia Marina would make Crete harder to isolate, allowing naval and air forces to concentrate on keeping it supplied. The island could then support attacks on Axis positions in the Aegean, Ionian, and Adriatic, including fuel supply positions. These military setbacks could affect Axis coalition decisions, although Mussolini's fall remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The transcript considers Mussolini's political weakness, possible reactions to defeats in Libya and Greece, German intervention, and the improved Allied ability to sustain Crete.

segments.summary: The counterfactual links a worse Taranto, a rapid loss of Libya, and a stalled Greek campaign to Mussolini's political vulnerability and Germany's choices in the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Releasing Ark Royal and Illustrious for other theatres
segments.body: Adding Dunkerque and Strasbourg to Prince of Wales, King George V, Hood, Renown, and Repulse would give the Allies seven fast capital ships at this stage of the scenario. With the Italian fleet badly damaged and Malta and Crete secure, the Mediterranean might also no longer need Ark Royal's striking power. Eagle could remain there, while Illustrious is a possible reinforcement for the Far East with maintenance support at Singapore. A refitted Ark Royal could work her air group alongside Victorious in the North Atlantic. This would place the carriers together before a German sortie instead of bringing Ark Royal north from Force H during the operation. The scenario still assumes the historical losses of Glorious and Courageous, so these deployment choices depend on the carriers remaining after those losses.

evidence.note: The scenario counts seven fast capital ships and considers Eagle, Ark Royal, Illustrious, and Victorious deployments while assuming Glorious and Courageous are still lost.

segments.summary: A weakened Italian fleet could release Ark Royal for the North Atlantic and Illustrious for the Far East while Eagle remains in the Mediterranean.

segments.title: More Atlantic capital ships against German raiders
segments.body: A larger Allied force in the North Atlantic could change German decisions about Operations Berlin and Rheinübung. Dunkerque and Strasbourg would join the British fast ships and make it easier to give Hood overdue maintenance before a German sortie. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau would be more likely to encounter a fast opponent capable of damaging or slowing them. Hitler's anger after their historical encounter with Renown illustrates how damage, even when ships escape, could restrict later operations. Bismarck might stay in port, sortie separately, or sail with both ships in a combined operation around May 1941. A combined German force could defeat a lone battleship escort and still suffer damage that exposed it to heavier Allied pursuers. Ark Royal and Victorious could launch joint strikes, with fast and heavy capital-ship groups following. The example envisages four or five ships in each Allied group, so a slowed German force could face roughly ten capital ships, although the actual battle and losses remain uncertain.

evidence.note: Additional fast ships permit Hood's maintenance and complicate German sortie choices, with damage exposing raiders to slower heavy ships.
A combined German sortie is considered against joint carrier strikes and two Allied capital-ship groups of roughly four or five ships each.

segments.summary: Dunkerque and Strasbourg could help contain German Atlantic raiders, free Hood for maintenance, and change whether Bismarck sails alone or with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau.

segments.title: Fast ships find the fight and heavy ships close in
segments.body: A more destructive Taranto raid could release the modernised Queen Elizabeth-class battleships Warspite, Queen Elizabeth, and Valiant from Mediterranean duties. They would strengthen the heavier force following the Allied fast capital ships in the Atlantic. The comparison is Somerville's Force A and Force B, with the faster group finding and engaging the enemy while the slower group moves up to finish the action. This is presented as an established British doctrinal approach. Part of the French argument for Dunkerque and Strasbourg had been that their speed could fill a Royal Navy shortage. Providing those ships would make France a more useful partner and help secure British support for the alliance.

evidence.note: The discussion links Queen Elizabeth-class redeployment to fast and heavy groups, Somerville's Force A and B, and the alliance rationale for the Dunkerque class.

segments.summary: Modernised Queen Elizabeths could support an Anglo-French fast force, using a doctrine in which fast ships engage the enemy before heavier ships arrive.

segments.title: French Indochina and a stronger Far East deterrent
segments.body: Free French control of Indochina means Japan would have to conquer Vietnam instead of obtaining it through pressure on Vichy authorities. An attack on Malaya or Singapore would then begin from farther back, and a Southeast Asian war might open with an invasion of Vietnam. That additional campaign would buy time for the Allies, while leaving an attack on Hawaii possible. French and British submarines and other ships could remain in the Far East because fewer had been withdrawn to the Mediterranean. Richelieu might also be completed in Britain or America and join the Allied battle line, although the timing is uncertain. The stronger Allied position would change Japan's military calculations without establishing whether it would prevent war.

evidence.note: The transcript considers uncertain completion of Richelieu, the need to conquer Vietnam, and a more distant starting point for Japanese operations against Malaya and Singapore.

segments.summary: Free French Indochina could force Japan to conquer Vietnam and begin an advance toward Malaya and Singapore from farther away, buying the Allies time.

segments.title: Why Japan might still choose war despite worse odds
segments.body: Many Japanese leaders did not expect a strong chance of winning the Pacific War. They believed Japan was already losing strategically in peacetime, so war appeared as the only gamble that offered any chance of changing the outcome. A Free French Indochina and larger Allied naval presence would worsen the odds. Those disadvantages might still fail to remove the political logic behind the decision. Stronger deterrence therefore does not automatically prevent war in this scenario.

evidence.note: The transcript argues that Japanese leaders could choose war despite expecting poor odds because they believed Japan was already losing the peace.

segments.summary: A stronger Allied Far East position might not deter Japan because its leaders saw peacetime trends as defeat and war as their only remaining gamble.

segments.title: How the French fleet changes the war without deciding it
segments.body: An all-Free-French fleet would change the forces available across several theatres, while leaving major Allied defeats on land in place. France and Norway would still have fallen, and Greece would probably fall too. Europe would still probably require a later Allied reinvasion. A shorter North African campaign and a stronger Mediterranean position would allow forces to serve elsewhere and reduce withdrawals from distant stations. More submarines and experienced crews would also support further Allied submarine construction, while stronger convoys could impede German U-boat expansion. Japan might delay its entry to build resources, although its choice remains uncertain. Detailed predictions stop around mid-1941 because later outcomes depend too heavily on the altered campaigns.

evidence.note: The scenario links a shorter Mediterranean campaign, submarine experience, reduced overseas withdrawals, and possible Japanese delay while preserving major land defeats and the likely need to reinvade Europe.
Detailed predictions are limited around mid-1941 because subsequent outcomes become too contingent.

segments.summary: The French fleet could reshape naval campaigns and release forces for other theatres, while a later Allied reinvasion of Europe would probably still be necessary.

segments.title: How early U-boat losses weaken later officer training
segments.body: Additional convoy escorts could affect German submarine expansion long after an individual encounter. Prospective U-boat commanders learned through patrols under an experienced officer before taking their own command. Losing a few more boats early in the war, even half a dozen in this example, could remove officers who would otherwise train the next group of commanders. A smaller intermediate generation would then struggle to support the later expansion. Sending inexperienced crews straight into submarine warfare would reduce effectiveness and increase the danger of losing boats through their own mistakes. The cumulative effect therefore depends on lost experience as well as lost hulls.

evidence.note: A few additional early losses remove officers who would train successive generations, while inexperienced crews risk losing their own boats.

segments.summary: Extra early U-boat losses could reduce the experienced officers available to train successive waves of new commanders.

segments.title: Which capital ships could reinforce the Far East in late 1941?
segments.body: If a German sortie and its ensuing battle were settled around May 1941, the scenario envisages a substantial Anglo-French carrier and fast-capital-ship force in the Far East by November. The possible pool comprises Richelieu, Dunkerque, Strasbourg, Hood, Renown, Repulse, King George V, Prince of Wales, and Duke of York. This is a pool of ships to choose from, with Richelieu's readiness uncertain. Losses against German capital ships would reduce availability, and some ships would still have to cover Tirpitz. Exceptionally effective carrier torpedo hits might disable German manoeuvring enough to limit Allied losses, although such a favourable outcome is considered unlikely. Queen Elizabeth, Valiant, and Warspite could provide a slower second echelon if freed from Mediterranean duties and spared Italian attacks at Alexandria. Nelson or Rodney are also suggested as possible additions.

evidence.note: The scenario proposes a late-1941 Far East force drawn from nine possible fast capital ships, with readiness and battle-loss caveats, a Tirpitz commitment, and possible slower reinforcements.

segments.summary: A hypothetical pool of nine fast capital ships gives the Allies more Far East options, subject to battle losses, ship readiness, and the need to contain Tirpitz.
